transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-04 14:30 PDT | Duration 73m | Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Desai, Marco Li (Redwood) // Sara Nguyen, Diego Ramos, Priya Patel, Tom Baker (Monarch)

Summary (auto): quick notes - this was a practical lab-style session; lots of command-level detail, intermittent crosstalk when network diagrams were being shared.

[00:00:00] Alex Kim: okay folks thanks for joining, um we wanted to run through the private VPC routing playbook and nail down failure modes that cause p99 spikes, especially when you run a private deployment behind PrivateLink and NAT.
[00:00:15] Sara Nguyen: yes thanks, uh our main pain is intermittent latency jumps during business hours, looks like sometimes requests go to a cold model, sometimes the kv cache misses and there's a huge jump.
[00:00:28] Diego Ramos: to add, we see more issues when cross-AZ failover happens, like a couple seconds extra which kills our realtime SLOs.
[00:00:35] Priya Desai: ok, so first clarification — are you using PrivateLink for control plane only, or data plane? and is egress via NAT gateway or an egress proxy?
[00:00:47] Tom Baker: currently control plane over PrivateLink, inference traffic flows out through our egress NAT gateway back to Redwood's dedicated endpoints; we also have an outbound proxy in front of the NAT for policy.
[00:01:01] Marco Li: right, that combination can produce hairpinning in some subnet layouts, esp if the source node's routing sends traffic out then immediately back in. That round trip goes through the customer's NAT and edge proxies adding ms to seconds depending on state.
[00:01:17] Priya Patel: and we have strict firewall state timeouts, so if the connections are short-lived they often teardown and need TCP handshake again which amplifies cold-kv misses.
[00:01:28] Alex Kim: good call. two knobs to consider: reduce hairpin by using interface endpoints/PrivateLink for data plane where possible, and second keep a pool of warmed connections at the edge or use persistent TCP or TLS pooling.
[00:01:44] Sara Nguyen: are there any gotchas with PrivateLink? we heard it can limit scaling or cause single-AZ bottlenecks.
[00:01:52] Priya Desai: yeah PrivateLink is single-AZ by nature per endpoint; you need multi-endpoint in multiple AZs and then do DNS or routing-based failover. we discussed cross-AZ endpoints earlier; the tricky thing is client routing — if the client's DNS cached to one AZ it won't automatically shift.
[00:02:06] Diego Ramos: that explains our failover microbursts — when AZ fails over, DNS TTLs and client cache cause a burst of new connections to the alternate endpoint, and NAT SNAT port exhaustion occurs on the egress gateway.
[00:02:20] Marco Li: exactly. recommended pattern: multi-AZ PrivateLink endpoints + client-side health check with short circuiting (circuit-breaker) and also ephemeral SNAT port management: rotate IPs or use multiple NAT gateways to spread ports.
[00:02:33] Sara Nguyen: we currently have one NAT GW per AZ. Tom, do we have elastic IPs floating?
[00:02:39] Tom Baker: yeah one per AZ, but not autopromoted, and the autoscaling for NAT is manual right now.
[00:02:44] Alex Kim: for a high-throughput inference workload we often suggest at least two NAT gateways per AZ or use Egress Load Balancer pattern to avoid port scarcity. also consider configuring tcp_tw_reuse and shortening TIME_WAIT on the egress nodes if your security team allows.
[00:02:59] Priya Patel: hmm security might be sensitive to changing kernel TCP settings, we'd need an exception and risk assessment.
[00:03:06] Alex Kim: understood. alternatives: use PrivateLink data plane so egress never leaves VPC — that removes SNAT entirely, but you must design endpoints across AZs and ensure your routing uses the nearest endpoint.
[00:03:18] Diego Ramos: what about DNS? we've been bitten by resolver inconsistencies. sometimes endpoints resolve to an AZ that has a problem.
[00:03:25] Marco Li: DNS TTL tuning is critical. use health-aware DNS or route53 weighted failover. within the VPC use the VPC resolver and set client TTL low (5-15s) for endpoints used in failover. but note low TTL increases DNS query load and can surface upstream resolver rate limits.
[00:03:40] Sara Nguyen: ok and KV cache behavior — Diego mentioned hotkeys — what's the recommended TTL and sharding?
[00:03:47] Priya Desai: first, identify hotkeys: if a small set of prompts drives 60% of traffic you want to pin them in the local node cache (pre-populate) and increase pin TTL or use an LRU with sticky reservations. second, use probabilistic early eviction to avoid thundering herd on expiration.
[00:04:05] Diego Ramos: we saw a cluster of misses when a cached key expired — then many parallel requests repopulate, causing increased model compute and IO contention.
[00:04:12] Alex Kim: mitigation options: 1) refresh-before-expire background refresher, 2) jittered TTLs so not all keys expire same time, 3) front-door admission control to queue or shed non-critical requests when backend latency is high.
[00:04:26] Tom Baker: refresh-before-expire sounds nice but increases steady-state traffic. is there a guideline for balancing refresh cost vs miss cost?
[00:04:34] Priya Desai: measure miss penalty — e.g., if a miss costs 200-600ms extra and refresh costs 10-30ms per key, then for keys above a threshold of hits/min do refresh. do the math. Marco has a small script we can share.
[00:04:46] Marco Li: yep I'll attach the hotkey analyzer script; it's a simple sliding-window frequency calculator.
[00:04:51] Alex Kim: switching to quantization — did you run low-precision profiles in production? any weird tail behavior?
[00:04:58] Diego Ramos: yes we trialed 8-bit and one 4-bit run. 4-bit had lower median but the p99 sometimes spiked due to extra kernel path fallback and occasional dequantize/validate steps in our runtime.
[00:05:11] Priya Desai: runtime kernel selection matters — when certain ops are missing optimized kernels the runtime falls back to slower code paths. we recommend profiling per model size and sequence length distribution and pinning quantization only for stable paths.
[00:05:25] Alex Kim: also worth using hybrid quantization where attention uses higher precision. This reduces p99 spikes but keeps cost savings.
[00:05:32] Sara Nguyen: observability — we need obvious signals to detect when it's a network-induced p99 vs a model-side problem.
[00:05:38] Marco Li: instrument both at edge and runtime: e2e traces with span tags for "dns_lookup", "tcp_connect", "tls_handshake", "kv_cache_hit", "runtime_infer". if kv_cache_hit false and tcp_connect high, that points to network. if runtime_infer high but tcp low, it's model.
[00:05:53] Diego Ramos: do you have sample dashboards? we want p50/p95/p99 broken down by path (privatelink vs nat) and by AZ.
[00:05:59] Alex Kim: yes we'll share a per-path latency dashboard template (grafana + prometheus queries) and a small script to synthesize split path traffic for testing.
[00:06:07] Priya Patel: security note — we need to see the audit log retention and key wrap details. can Redwood show a sample KMS integration and audit trails?
[00:06:14] Alex Kim: yes, we'll include KMS/HSM integration notes and a sample audit log with masked tokens, plus SOC2 packet.
[00:06:21] Sara Nguyen: ok recap? also who will own the pilot run?
[00:06:24] Alex Kim: recap: Redwood will provide NAT/proxy test plan, runtime tuning guide, dashboard templates, and hotkey analyzer; Monarch will export VPC route tables and designate a pilot window. Owner: Alex for Redwood deliverables, Sara for Monarch artifacts.
[00:06:41] Tom Baker: I'll carve out time for pilot infra.
[00:06:44] Diego Ramos: one more quick thing — can Redwood vendor run a small controlled load (tenants isolated) to simulate multi-tenant behavior?
[00:06:51] Alex Kim: yes, we can spin a controlled synthetic workload from Redwood infra to hit your PrivateLink endpoints and we can share results.
[00:06:58] Priya Desai: action items reiterated in chat. thanks everyone.
[00:07:03] Sara Nguyen: thanks, that was helpful, we'll await the doc pack.

End of recording.
